title: Oxygen as a prescribed drug: target ranges 94-98% and 88-92%
blurb: Choose the right saturation target for each adult, spot who is at risk of hypercapnia and know when oximetry misleads you.
question: Mr Okafor, 71, has severe COPD and was given oxygen at 15 L/min by reservoir mask in the ambulance. On the ward his SpO2 is 99% and he is becoming drowsy. What target range should guide his oxygen, and what is the danger?

teach.h: Oxygen is a drug with a target
teach.body: Formally: oxygen is a treatment for hypoxaemia, not for breathlessness, and should be prescribed to a target saturation range rather than a fixed concentration (BTS 2017). In plain English: you are aiming for a number on the oximeter, not a number on the flowmeter. Most acutely ill adults are aimed at 94–98%. People at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure are aimed at 88–92% until blood gases show otherwise.
teach.cite: BTS guideline for oxygen use in adults 2017 (still current, BTS 2019 statement)

teach.h: The two target ranges on one SpO2 scale
teach.caption: Both ranges are prescribed on the drug chart or electronic system. Saturation above the target range is also outside target.

children.label: Reservoir mask 15 L/min
children.sub: e.g. shock, sepsis, major trauma; then titrate

teach.caption: A person with COPD who is critically ill (e.g. shock, sepsis, major trauma) gets the same initial high-concentration oxygen as anyone else pending gases.

teach.h: Who is at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure
head: Condition
Example
teach.caption: BTS 2017 Table 4. Some people carry an oxygen alert card showing their own target from previous blood gases.

teach.h: Why too much oxygen harms some people
teach.body: In someone at risk, high-concentration oxygen can raise carbon dioxide and cause respiratory acidosis: they become drowsy, confused or flushed while the oximeter looks reassuring. So aim for 88–92% and check blood gases. If the PCO2 is normal, the target can move to 94–98% (unless they have needed NIV or invasive ventilation before), and gases are rechecked 30–60 minutes after any change.

teach.h: Situations with their own oxygen rules
teach.caption: CG95 1.2.3.3 (chest pain), NG128 1.5.1 (stroke), BTS 2017 Table 1 (carbon monoxide).

teach.h: What the oximeter cannot tell you

rows.label: A fall of 3% or more within range

teach.note: Before increasing oxygen for a low reading, first check the delivery system and the oximeter for faults (BTS W16).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr Okafor on a respiratory ward
teach.body: Mr Okafor has severe COPD. His SpO2 is 99% on a reservoir mask and he is drowsy: he is above his 88–92% target and may be retaining CO2. Nurse Priya asks for urgent medical review and blood gases. She does not simply remove the oxygen: BTS warns that sudden cessation can cause life-threatening rebound hypoxaemia. Instead oxygen is stepped down (e.g. 24% or 28% Venturi) to the lowest level that keeps him at 88–92%.
teach.cite: BTS 2017: management of hypercapnia due to excessive oxygen

teach.text: A normal or high SpO2 does NOT rule out danger. In COPD it can hide rising CO2; in carbon monoxide poisoning the oximeter cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. And 88–92% is the at-risk target, not the target for every adult with a respiratory problem.

items.label: target for most acutely ill adults
target if at risk of hypercapnia, pending gases
reservoir mask in critical illness or SpO2 below 85%
recheck blood gases after a change (at-risk group)

items: Oxygen treats hypoxaemia, not breathlessness, and is prescribed to a target range.
94–98% for most adults; 88–92% for COPD and other hypercapnia risks until gases guide you.
Critical illness: reservoir mask 15 L/min first, whatever the diagnosis, then titrate.
ACS and stroke: no routine oxygen. CO poisoning: maximum oxygen, ignore the oximeter reading.
Over-oxygenation in at-risk patients: step down, do not stop abruptly, get gases.

summary: You can now prescribe-check and titrate oxygen against the right target range, 94–98% or 88–92%, and identify who is at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. You also know the exceptions (critical illness, ACS, stroke, carbon monoxide) and the limits of pulse oximetry.

A.q: What is the usual target oxygen saturation range for an acutely ill adult with pneumonia and no risk factors for hypercapnia?
A.why: BTS 2017 recommends a target of 94–98% for most acutely ill adults.

whyNot.0: 88–92% is the target for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
whyNot.1: 92–96% is not a BTS target range; the lower limit for most adults is 94%.
whyNot.3: Aiming for up to 100% is not recommended for most adults; the upper limit is 98%.

A.q: Which patient is most likely to need an initial target saturation of 88–92%?
options: A man with a BMI of 44 kg/m²
A woman with community-acquired pneumonia
A man with a suspected pulmonary embolism
A woman with acute heart failure
A.why: Morbid obesity (BMI above 40 kg/m²) is one of the BTS risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure, alongside COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, neuromuscular disease and chest wall deformity.

whyNot.1: Pneumonia without hypercapnia risk factors has a target of 94–98%.
whyNot.2: Pulmonary embolism alone is not a hypercapnia risk; the target is 94–98%.
whyNot.3: Acute heart failure alone does not place someone in the BTS at-risk group.

A.q: A man is brought in after a house fire with suspected carbon monoxide poisoning. His SpO2 reads 99%. How should the nurse interpret this reading?
options: It confirms he has adequate oxygenation
It shows oxygen can be titrated down
It is unreliable for carboxyhaemoglobin
It means a blood gas is not needed
A.why: Pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a normal or high reading should be disregarded. Give as much oxygen as possible (BTS 2017 Table 1).

whyNot.0: A high reading in CO poisoning can coexist with serious tissue hypoxia.
whyNot.1: CO poisoning needs as much oxygen as possible, not titration to a reading.
whyNot.3: Carboxyhaemoglobin levels must be checked on a blood sample.

B.q: A woman with chest pain and suspected ACS has an SpO2 of 97% on air. She has no lung disease. What is the most appropriate approach to oxygen?
options: Give 2 L/min by nasal cannulae
Give 15 L/min by reservoir mask
Give 28% oxygen by Venturi mask
Monitor SpO2, no oxygen for now
B.why: CG95 1.2.3.3: do not routinely give oxygen in suspected ACS. Monitor SpO2 and offer oxygen if it falls below 94% (target 94–98%).

whyNot.0: Low-flow oxygen is still routine oxygen, which is not recommended when SpO2 is 97%.
whyNot.1: High-concentration oxygen may harm non-hypoxaemic patients with ACS.
whyNot.2: A Venturi mask is for controlled oxygen in hypoxaemic at-risk patients, not for normal saturations.

B.q: A patient's SpO2 has dropped from 96% to 90% on 2 L/min nasal cannulae. Before increasing the oxygen, what should the nurse check first?
options: The tubing, flowmeter and oximeter probe
The most recent full blood count results
The patient's 24-hour fluid balance
The time of the last medication round
B.why: BTS W16: if saturation is below the target range, first check all aspects of the delivery system and the oximeter for faults, then increase oxygen and seek review as needed.

whyNot.1: Anaemia matters for oxygen delivery, but equipment faults are checked first.
whyNot.2: Fluid balance does not explain a sudden fall and does not come first.
whyNot.3: The medication round timing does not explain a falling saturation.

B.q: Blood gases for a patient with COPD on a 24% Venturi mask show a normal PCO2. He has never needed NIV or ventilation. What should happen to his target range?
options: Keep it at 88–92% for the whole admission
Change it to 94–98% and recheck gases
Change it to 92–96% with no further gases
Stop oxygen and repeat gases tomorrow
B.why: BTS Table 4: adjust the target to 94–98% if the PCO2 is normal (unless there is a history of NIV or invasive ventilation) and recheck blood gases after 30–60 minutes.

whyNot.0: A normal PCO2 without previous NIV allows the standard target.
whyNot.2: 92–96% is not a BTS target, and gases are rechecked after a change.
whyNot.3: Oxygen is weaned against the target, not stopped pending a next-day gas.

C.q: Mr Hale, 74, has COPD and was given high-flow oxygen by paramedics. His SpO2 is 98%, his respiratory rate has fallen and he is difficult to rouse. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Remove the oxygen and recheck SpO2 in an hour
Continue the oxygen as SpO2 is in normal range
Step oxygen down to keep 88–92% and get gases
Sit him upright and increase the oxygen flow
C.why: Drowsiness and slowing breathing on high-flow oxygen suggest hypercapnia. BTS: step oxygen down to the lowest level that maintains 88–92%, get urgent blood gases and medical review. Sudden cessation risks rebound hypoxaemia.

whyNot.0: Abruptly stopping oxygen can cause life-threatening rebound hypoxaemia.
whyNot.1: 98% is above his 88–92% target and his drowsiness suggests CO2 retention.
whyNot.3: More oxygen would worsen the hypercapnia.

C.q: A woman with known COPD develops septic shock on the ward. Her blood gas results are not yet available. Which initial oxygen approach is correct?
options: 24% Venturi mask aiming for 88–92% SpO2
High-concentration reservoir mask
Nasal cannulae at 1–2 L/min
28% Venturi mask until blood gases
C.why: In critical illness, including shock and sepsis, at-risk patients receive the same initial high-concentration oxygen as other critically ill patients pending blood gases (BTS 2017 Table 1).

whyNot.0: Controlled oxygen is not the initial approach in septic shock, even with COPD.
whyNot.2: Low-flow cannulae are inadequate initial oxygen in critical illness.
whyNot.3: A 28% Venturi mask is for stable at-risk patients, not septic shock.

C.q: Mr Diallo, 66, with an acute ischaemic stroke, has an SpO2 of 96% on air. A student suggests oxygen 'to protect his brain'. What is the best reply?
options: Give 2 L/min to keep SpO2 above 98%
Give oxygen via a simple face mask
Give oxygen as his SpO2 is below 97%
Monitor SpO2; give oxygen below 95%
C.why: NG128 1.5.1: give supplemental oxygen to people with acute stroke only if their oxygen saturation drops below 95%. Routine oxygen is not recommended.

whyNot.0: Routine oxygen to push SpO2 above 98% is not recommended after stroke.
whyNot.1: A face mask is still routine oxygen in a non-hypoxaemic patient.
whyNot.2: 97% is not the NG128 threshold; oxygen is given if SpO2 drops below 95%.

reteach.title: Two lanes on the oximeter
reteach.question: Picture an oximeter screen with two coloured lanes. How do you decide which lane a patient should travel in?

blocks.body: Every adult on oxygen travels in a lane. The wide green lane is 94–98%, for almost everyone. The amber lane, 88–92%, is for people whose breathing drive can fail with too much oxygen: COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, neuromuscular disease, chest wall deformity and morbid obesity. You steer with the oxygen device until the patient sits in their lane. Leaving the lane on either side is a problem.

blocks.h: At-risk patient: steering into the amber lane

blocks.text: Critical illness overrides the amber lane: shock, sepsis or major trauma in someone with COPD still starts with a reservoir mask at 15 L/min pending gases.

explain.body: Most acutely ill adults are aimed at 94–98% (BTS 2017). Below 85%, start with a reservoir mask at 15 L/min; otherwise nasal cannulae or a simple face mask, titrated to the range.

test.q: A hypoxaemic adult with no hypercapnia risk has an SpO2 of 83%. What should oxygen therapy start with?
options: Nasal cannulae at 2 L/min
Reservoir mask at 15 L/min
24% Venturi mask at 2 L/min
Simple face mask at 5 L/min
test.why: BTS 2017: if SpO2 is below 85% in a patient not at risk of hypercapnia, start with a reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then titrate to 94–98%.

whyNot.0: Nasal cannulae are used when SpO2 is 85% or above.
whyNot.2: A 24% Venturi mask is for at-risk patients, not this patient.
whyNot.3: A simple face mask is used when SpO2 is 85% or above.

explain.body: 88–92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, pending blood gases: COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, neuromuscular disease, chest wall deformity, morbid obesity (BMI above 40).

test.q: Which condition places an adult in the BTS group at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
options: Well-controlled asthma
Community-acquired pneumonia
Motor neurone disease
Pulmonary embolism
test.why: Neuromuscular disease (such as motor neurone disease) is a BTS risk factor for hypercapnic respiratory failure.

whyNot.0: Asthma is managed with a 94–98% target.
whyNot.1: Pneumonia without other risk factors has a 94–98% target.
whyNot.3: Pulmonary embolism alone has a 94–98% target.

explain.body: Most people with ACS or stroke are not hypoxaemic, and unnecessary high-concentration oxygen may do harm. Chest pain: oxygen if SpO2 below 94% (CG95). Stroke: oxygen if SpO2 below 95% (NG128).

test.q: A man with central chest pain and a suspected MI has an SpO2 of 95% on air and no lung disease. What is correct about oxygen?
options: Give 15 L/min for any suspected MI
Give oxygen if SpO2 falls below 94%
Give 4 L/min to reduce infarct size
Give oxygen if SpO2 falls below 97%
test.why: CG95 1.2.3.3: do not routinely give oxygen; offer it if SpO2 is below 94% (aiming for 94–98%) in people not at risk of hypercapnia.

whyNot.0: High-flow oxygen is not routine in suspected MI.
whyNot.2: Unnecessary oxygen may increase infarct size rather than reduce it.

explain.body: Oximetry gives no information about PCO2 or pH, reads falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning, and may over-estimate saturation in people with darker skin. Treat the patient, not the number.

test.q: A patient with COPD has an SpO2 of 91% but is newly confused and drowsy. What does the nurse need to establish?
options: Whether the oximeter probe is cold
Whether the PCO2 and pH are abnormal
Whether SpO2 is above 88% breathing air
Whether the flow should be raised
test.why: Pulse oximetry gives no information on carbon dioxide or pH. New drowsiness or confusion in an at-risk patient needs blood gases to look for hypercapnia and acidosis.

whyNot.0: A cold probe affects the reading, but the clinical change needs a blood gas.
whyNot.2: SpO2 on air does not show CO2 retention.
